correctness.rationale:
For \(C\geq 2B\), each summand beyond the constant in \(T_n/b^n\) is even because the central binomial factor is even. For \(C\leq 2B-2\), the exact normalized factorial expansion yields \(
u_2(	ext{term}_j)\geq j(2B-C-2)+s_2(j)\geq1\); for \(j\geq2\) the falling factorial is even and the valuation is at least three. Legendre's formula gives \(
u_2 inom{2m}{m}=s_2(m)\), proving the unrestricted valuation and first correction modulo four. At the critical line, explicit \(b=2^B3\) and \(c=2^{2B-1}(2^r-9)\) make \(
u_2(T_2)=2B+r\); \(c=-9\cdot2^{2B-1}\) makes \(T_2=0\). The dyadic histogram follows by counting Hamming weights. Independent finite recurrence checks corroborate the proof but cannot establish all cases.

evidence: Noe's Theorem 8.5 supplies a general prime-divisibility digit criterion; that broader qualitative condition has only yes/no valuation content.
Sun's congruence sums cover many generalized-coefficient values at odd primes and include T_n(2,1), but do not state the two-adic normalized unit or boundary construction.
The new formula gives the exact finite exponent, not merely whether a prime divides the coefficient.
The Wang–Sun parametric theorems are weighted sums modulo squares of odd primes and do not give an exact two-adic valuation of a single coefficient.

Theorem 3 proves v_p(P_n(r)) for any rational r of valuation >=1; the 2-adic part plus T_n(b,c)=d^(n/2)P_n(b/sqrt(d)) implies the matching valuation formula for rational-square d and sufficiently divisible argument.
broader_coverage.reasoning: Stronger general prime-divisibility coverage is acknowledged: it does not logically imply a fixed exact valuation or a mod-four normalized odd part. Even full knowledge of mod-two behavior cannot distinguish the phases or sharp boundary. This strong theorem covers a genuine special subfamily of the proposed valuation law when d is a rational square and the Legendre argument is sufficiently 2-adically divisible. It does not directly cover arbitrary nonsquare d (argument algebraic, not rational), the low-regime edge with argument valuation below one, or any normalized-unit congruence modulo four. The covered subclass is not claimed as independent novelty.

originality.rationale: Source-level comparison distinguishes the known coefficient definition, Noe's modulo-two and general prime-divisibility theorems, and Sun's central-binomial special case from the new all-index exact two-adic valuation phase formula plus first mod-four normalized unit and sharp boundary construction. The 2022 Mao–Liu abstract addresses odd-prime sums and its inaccessible full text remains a priority risk. Mathematical-record searches returned no stronger covering statement, but cannot prove historical uniqueness. Alekseyev et al. (2025) Theorem 3 is stronger on rational-argument Legendre valuations; it implies the valuation component on the appropriate rational-square-discriminant subclass, which is explicitly acknowledged. It does not state the full nonsquare family or mod-four normalized unit.
residual_risks: Unlocated earlier work may state the same all-index two-adic phase under Legendre polynomial or Newton polygon terminology.
The full 2022 Mao–Liu paper was inaccessible; abstract-only inspection does not prove noncoverage of its entire contents.
An exact formula for the critical line beyond the explicitly demonstrated nonuniformity is not provided.

An extension of the 2025 rational-argument Legendre valuation theorem to all relevant algebraic arguments could subsume part of the valuation formula; no such extension is established by the inspected theorem.

value.rationale: The generalized family has an established history of divisibility and congruence study. A uniform coefficient-valuation phase diagram for arbitrary n and nonzero b,c is a natural complete classification outside a single sharp line; it resolves all primitive pairs, adds an exact mod-four normalized-unit correction, and identifies explicit failure of valuation-only control at the boundary. The binomial all-depth histogram is a substantive consequence of an infinite coefficient classification, not a freestanding cherry-picked numerical slice. No claim of a broader theorem for all primes is made.
